title: The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself
gist: Hugging Face's Yuvraj Sharma used the ML-Intern agent mode in HuggingChat to build six public custom models (fine-tunes, LoRAs, distillations) in days for about USD 103 total compute, e.g., a 0.8B CPU-capable distillation of Qwen-Image 2.1's 9B prompt rewriter for ~USD 16. Key lessons: detailed prompts with verified facts, mandatory baselines, smoke tests and hard budget caps.

insights.claim: Six custom models built by Hugging Face's ML-Intern agent, from fine-tunes to distillations, cost about USD 103 in total GPU/CPU compute, with individual projects ranging from USD 1.90 to USD 37.
insights.speaker: yuvraj sharma
insights.so_what: Agent-driven training collapses the cost of bespoke models, expanding the long tail of niche models and Hub compute demand.

insights.claim: ML-Intern plans work, asks for a budget before spending, runs a small test, then trains, evaluates and publishes on Hugging Face hardware, starting each task with a zero-dollar budget that requires user permission for paid jobs.
insights.speaker: yuvraj sharma
insights.so_what: Hugging Face is monetizing agentic workflows through its own compute, a new revenue lever beyond hosting.
insights.locator: At the end of the prompt

insights.claim: Projects ran as many cloud jobs with failures auto-resubmitted, e.g., the camera-angle LoRA took about half a day and 48 jobs and Doodle-in took a little over a day and 59 jobs.
insights.speaker: yuvraj sharma
insights.so_what: Agents tolerate and fix infra failures cheaply, reducing ML engineer time per model.
insights.locator: 3. A model that does a new trick

insights.claim: The author's prompts grew from about 450 words to about 2,000 by the sixth project, including a 'Verified facts, do not re-derive' section so the agent spends budget on work instead of rediscovery.
insights.speaker: yuvraj sharma
insights.so_what: Effective agent use still depends on heavy, expert prompt specification; human expertise remains a bottleneck.

insights.claim: Two prompt elements are critical: requesting a zero-shot baseline before training and a smoke test with a check (e.g., 50 steps then verifying weights changed) before paying for the full run.
insights.speaker: yuvraj sharma
insights.so_what: Baseline and smoke-test discipline is the guardrail that makes autonomous training trustworthy and cheap.
insights.locator: Two lines in the prompt are critical.

insights.claim: A 0.8B student of Qwen-Image 2.1's official 9B prompt rewriter (which needs ~20 GB memory) runs on a CPU, returns valid output 99.7% of the time and uses about a quarter of the teacher's tokens, for about USD 16 of compute.
insights.speaker: yuvraj sharma
insights.so_what: Cheap distillation erodes the moat of large first-party components and pushes inference to edge/CPU.
insights.quote: It returns valid output 99.7% of the time and uses about a quarter of the teacher's tokens.
insights.locator: Last week, I wanted a small version

insights.claim: The rewriter pipeline generated 8,797 requests, had the 9B teacher rewrite them on one A100 in 2h37m (~USD 6.50), filtered to 1,840 examples, and trained 0.8B and 2B students in 12 and 18 minutes on an A10G for USD 0.75 combined; the 0.8B ships as an 812 MB GGUF.
insights.speaker: yuvraj sharma
insights.so_what: Teacher labeling dominates distillation cost; student training is nearly free.
insights.locator: 4. A model that fits your device

insights.claim: Distilling the 260M-parameter Agate Preview 002 text-to-image model from 50 guided steps (100 network passes) to 4 steps produced a student that beat the teacher at 4 steps on GenEval and FID; a second run lifted GenEval from 0.509 to 0.536 vs the teacher's 0.563 at 50 steps, for about USD 37 total, and was exported to ONNX for browsers.
insights.speaker: yuvraj sharma
insights.so_what: In-browser image generation becomes viable via cheap step distillation, shifting compute from cloud to client.

insights.claim: Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-2B on 3,017 citrus disease images raised correct diagnosis on 335 test photos from 14.9% to 52.8% after two epochs on one A10G, for about USD 1.90.
insights.speaker: yuvraj sharma
insights.so_what: Domain-specialized small VLMs can more than triple general-model accuracy for pennies, favoring vertical AI applications.
insights.locator: 1. A model that knows your field

insights.claim: Days after Qwen-Image 2.1's release no community camera-angle LoRA existed, so the agent rendered 24,722 transparent images of Google Scanned Objects and trained one in ~90 minutes on an A100 for ~USD 3.75 of training.
insights.speaker: yuvraj sharma
insights.so_what: Agents let individuals fill ecosystem gaps right after model releases, accelerating open-model ecosystem maturity.
insights.locator: 3. A model that does a new trick

insights.claim: The Doodle-in LoRA, trained on 6,042 synthetic pairs built with LaMa inpainting on Open Images, placed 67.5% of objects where drawn at 4.7 seconds per edit, with unseen classes performing as reliably as seen ones (65.0% vs 64.2%).
insights.speaker: yuvraj sharma
insights.so_what: Synthetic-data generation by agents can create training sets where no dataset exists.

insights.claim: A Huggy LoRA on FLUX.2 klein base 4B was fully on-model at step 200 but from step 500 its style bled into unrelated prompts, showing checkpoint selection matters.
insights.speaker: yuvraj sharma
insights.so_what: Overfitting risk persists even in automated pipelines; evaluation per checkpoint is key.
insights.locator: 2. A model that draws your character
